analysis.one_liner: Permanently restores the estate tax with a $5 million exemption and a 35% top rate.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 47 cosponsors from both parties, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was filed and never received a hearing or vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2001 tax law had scheduled the estate tax to disappear entirely for one year in 2010 and then snap back in 2011 to a $1 million exemption and a 55% rate. This bill would cancel both: it keeps the estate tax permanently, but on much gentler terms — an exemption growing from $3.5 million to $5 million and a top rate falling from 45% to 35%. Estates below the exemption would owe nothing; only the largest inheritances would be taxed, and at a lower rate than before 2001. It was a bipartisan compromise meant to end the uncertainty, and it never got a hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $3.5 million (rising to $5 million) benefit most: they escape the higher pre-2001 rates that were scheduled to return in 2011 and get a top rate of 35% instead of 55%. Supporters also argued the public gains from certainty — no one-year repeal in 2010 and no cliff in 2011 — and from keeping any estate tax on the largest fortunes at all.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the provisions of the 2001 Bush tax law that eliminated the estate tax for one year and cancels that law's sunset for its estate tax title, so the estate tax never disappears and never snaps back to pre-2001 levels.
It sets the estate tax exemption at $3.5 million immediately, rising gradually to $5 million by 2019 with inflation adjustments after that, so any estate below those amounts owes no estate tax.
It lowers the top estate tax rate gradually from 45% to 35%, giving wealthy families a permanently lower rate than either the 2009 law (45%) or the pre-2001 law (55%).

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost of the lower rate and larger exemption compared with pre-2001 law — revenue that would otherwise come from the estates of the wealthiest households. State governments also lose, because the bill phases out the federal deduction for state death taxes to zero by 2019.

drawbacks.text: Compared with the pre-2001 law that would otherwise have returned in 2011, the bill is a large tax cut for wealthy families: the exemption grows to $5 million (versus $1 million) and the top rate falls to 35% (versus 55%), reducing federal revenue from the estates of the wealthiest households.
The bill phases out the federal deduction for state death taxes to zero by 2019, which would reduce state tax collections on large estates and pressure state budgets.

The terms phase in over a decade on a year-by-year schedule of rates and exemptions, which would have made planning difficult during the transition and locked in each step only as future Congresses let it stand.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest point is that it would have ended the uncertainty around the estate tax — preventing a total repeal in 2010 and a snap back to a $1 million exemption and 55% rate in 2011 — while keeping a tax on the largest inheritances on the books [S2][S3]. Its serious drawback is the price it paid for that compromise: a 35% top rate and a $5 million exemption are far more generous than pre-2001 law, costing federal revenue that funds public services, and the phaseout of the state death tax deduction shifts a further cost onto state budgets [S2][S3]. It is a genuine middle ground — better for the public than full repeal, worse than the historical estate tax — and it was never given a vote in either direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Shelley Berkley introduced the bill on October 22, 2009, joined as original co-leads by Reps. Kevin Brady of Texas, Danny Davis of Alabama, and Devin Nunes of California.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — between that referral and the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

The bill's purpose was to repeal the one-year estate tax repeal scheduled for 2010 under the 2001 Bush tax law and replace it with a permanent estate tax: a $5 million exemption and 35% top rate by 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs of the largest estates: because no compromise passed in time, 2010 arrived with no estate tax at all, and the eventual settlement years later was set on terms at least as generous as this bill proposed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was split across both parties: of 47 cosponsors, 25 were Republicans and 22 were Democrats, and the original co-lead group paired two Democrats with two Republicans.

industries.industry: Heirs of the wealthiest households (estates over $3.5 million)
industries.note: The bill keeps the estate tax alive, which these families opposed, but locks in a much lighter version of it: a $5 million exemption and a 35% top rate versus the $1 million and 55% that pre-2001 law would have restored. Their gain comes directly out of federal revenue.
The bill phases out the federal deduction for state death taxes to zero by 2019, reducing what states collect on large estates. That cost lands on state budgets and the services they fund.

industries.industry: Federal treasury and the public services it funds
industries.note: Relative to a full repeal of the estate tax, the bill preserves revenue from the largest inheritances for federal spending. Relative to pre-2001 law, it gives away much of that revenue through the lower rate and bigger exemption.
